subject: Medieval History
sub_topic: Rajput states — Amber, Marwar, Mewar, Bikaner

concepts.name: Rajput Policy of Akbar: Matrimonial Alliances and Administrative Integration
key_dimensions: Which Rajput clans accepted Mughal matrimonial alliances vs. those who refused (Mewar as the key exception)
Administrative benefits granted to allied Rajputs — mansabs, governorships, military commands
Contrast with Aurangzeb's reversal of Akbar's conciliatory Rajput policy
UPSC trap: Distinguishing which rulers personally married into Mughal family vs. merely submitted politically

concepts.name: Amber (Kachwaha Clan): Rise to Mughal Partnership
key_dimensions: Bharmal's submission to Akbar (1562) as the foundational event — first major Rajput chief to ally
Role of Raja Man Singh I as Mughal commander — Bengal, Bihar, Kabul campaigns
Amber's transformation into Jaipur under Sawai Jai Singh II — urban planning and astronomical contributions
UPSC trap: Conflating Amber (medieval state) with Jaipur (18th century successor) in timeline questions

concepts.name: Man Singh I of Amber: Military and Administrative Significance
key_dimensions: Appointed governor of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa and Kabul — extent of Mughal trust in a Rajput noble
Role in suppressing the Ustad revolt and campaigns in Deccan
Construction of Man Singh Palace at Gwalior and Vrindavan temples — cultural patronage
UPSC trap: Man Singh I (Akbar's general) vs. Man Singh II (who signed instrument of accession to India in 1949)

concepts.name: Mewar (Sisodia Clan): Persistent Resistance to Mughal Authority
key_dimensions: Sequence of rulers — Rana Sanga, Udai Singh II, Maharana Pratap, Amar Singh I — each with distinct posture toward Mughals
Why Mewar alone among major Rajput states refused matrimonial alliance with Mughals for longest period
Treaty of 1615 (Amar Singh I with Jahangir) — terms, significance, and what Mewar retained vs. conceded
UPSC trap: Rana Sanga fought against Babur (Khanwa 1527) while other Rajputs allied — pre-Mughal vs. Mughal-era resistance conflation

concepts.name: Battle of Haldighati (1576): Causes, Conduct, and Contested Outcomes
key_dimensions: Mughal force commanded by Man Singh I (Amber) vs. Maharana Pratap — Rajput-on-Rajput dimension
Tactical outcome debated — Pratap retreated but was not captured; Mughals did not consolidate Mewar
Role of Hakim Khan Sur (Afghan commander) in Pratap's forces — composite nature of resistance
UPSC trap: Often asked as 'decisive Mughal victory' — actually inconclusive; Pratap recovered Mewar territories later

concepts.name: Maharana Pratap: Guerrilla Resistance and the Mewar Recovery
key_dimensions: Post-Haldighati phase — use of Aravalli hills, guerrilla tactics, Bhil tribal support
Recovery of most of Mewar (except Chittor and Mandalgarh) by 1585 during Akbar's northwest preoccupation
Patronage role — cultural and symbolic importance as a Hindu Rajput resistor in historiography
UPSC trap: Pratap died in 1597 — not captured or killed in battle; his son Amar Singh eventually made peace

concepts.name: Marwar (Rathore Clan): Mughal Relations and the Succession Crisis of 1678
key_dimensions: Jaswant Singh I's complex loyalty — fought for Shah Jahan, then Dara Shikoh at Dharmat (1658), later served Aurangzeb
Aurangzeb's annexation of Marwar after Jaswant Singh's death (1678) — refusal to recognize infant Ajit Singh
Durga Das Rathore's role in protecting Ajit Singh and keeping resistance alive — key individual
UPSC trap: The 1678 crisis was a turning point in Mughal-Rajput relations, not merely a local dispute — linked to Aurangzeb's broader anti-Rajput shift

concepts.name: Rathor-Sisodia Alliance and the Marwar-Mewar-Mughal Triangle
key_dimensions: Post-1678 alliance between Marwar and Mewar against Aurangzeb — rare united Rajput front
Impact on Mughal military resources — Aurangzeb fighting simultaneously in Deccan and Rajputana
Eventual settlement under Bahadur Shah I (1707) — Ajit Singh recognized, Marwar restored
UPSC trap: This alliance is often overlooked in favor of individual state histories; its collective impact on Mughal decline is a frequent analytical question

concepts.name: Bikaner (Rathore Branch): Founding, Dynasty, and Mughal Service
key_dimensions: Founded by Rao Bika (son of Rao Jodha of Marwar) in 1488 — a cadet branch of Rathores, not a separate clan
Rai Singh of Bikaner — prominent Mughal mansabdar under Akbar and Jahangir; built Junagarh Fort
Bikaner's geographic role — Thar Desert frontier, trade routes to Sindh and Central Asia
UPSC trap: Bikaner Rathores vs. Marwar Rathores — same clan, different branches; confusion in 'which Rajput state' questions

concepts.name: Rai Singh of Bikaner: Mansabdari Career and Fort Construction
key_dimensions: One of the highest-ranking Rajput mansabdars under Akbar — 5000 zat rank
Military campaigns: Gujarat, Deccan, Kabul — breadth of Mughal imperial service
Junagarh Fort (1589–94) — architectural significance, never captured by enemy forces
UPSC trap: Rai Singh of Bikaner vs. Man Singh of Amber — both high-ranking Rajput commanders under Akbar, often confused

concepts.name: Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber/Jaipur: Scientific, Urban, and Political Legacy
key_dimensions: Construction of five Jantar Mantar observatories — Jaipur, Delhi, Varanasi, Ujjain, Mathura — astronomical significance
Founding of Jaipur (1727) — planned city, grid layout, influence of Euclid and Ptolemy
Political role in late Mughal period — attempted Rajput confederation; Mughal kingmaker briefly
UPSC trap: Jantar Mantar in Delhi often associated with Delhi alone — Jaipur's is the largest and best preserved

concepts.name: Chittor and Its Symbolism: Jauhars and Rajput Honor Culture
key_dimensions: Three sacks of Chittor — Alauddin Khalji (1303), Bahadur Shah of Gujarat (1535), Akbar (1568)
Jauhar practice — mass self-immolation by Rajput women; Padmini's jauhar (1303) as legendary example
Akbar's massacre at Chittor (1568) — Abul Fazl records 30,000 killed; Akbar's rare act of large-scale killing
UPSC trap: Chittor was the capital of Mewar but Akbar captured it in 1568 — Udai Singh II had already shifted to Udaipur (founded 1559)

concepts.name: Rajput Administrative and Revenue System: Internal Governance
key_dimensions: Jagir system within Rajput states — thikanas, bhomia chiefs, hierarchical land grants
Role of nobles (sardars/thakurs) in military obligation to the ruling clan
Patta and qabuliyat equivalents in Rajput states vs. Mughal revenue administration
UPSC trap: Rajput internal feudalism is often contrasted with Mughal centralization — understanding where they overlapped is key for analytical questions

concepts.name: Rajput Clan Identity and the Myth of Rajput Origins
key_dimensions: Agnikula origin myth — Pratiharas, Paramaras, Chahamanas, Chalukyas — fire-born lineages
Suryavanshi (solar) vs. Chandravanshi (lunar) lineages — Sisodias (Suryavanshi), Kachwaha (Suryavanshi), Rathores (Suryavanshi)
Colonial historiography (Tod's Annals) vs. modern revisionist views on Rajput identity construction
UPSC trap: All four major Rajput states in this subtopic are Suryavanshi — Chandravanshi distinction is a trap option

concepts.name: Battle of Khanwa (1527): Rana Sanga, Babur, and Rajput Political Calculations
key_dimensions: Rana Sanga of Mewar initially invited Babur to defeat Ibrahim Lodi — later realized threat of Mughal permanence
Coalition at Khanwa — Rajputs, Afghan chiefs, Mahmud Lodi — diverse anti-Babur front
Babur's declaration of jihad and use of artillery — tactical vs. ideological dimensions
UPSC trap: Khanwa (1527) is often treated as a footnote to Panipat I (1526) but is equally decisive for Rajput and Afghan power consolidation

concepts.name: Mewar-Mughal Treaty of 1615 (Jahangir–Amar Singh I): Terms and Implications
key_dimensions: Amar Singh surrendered suzerainty but Mewar princes never required to personally attend Mughal court or give daughters in marriage
Chittor not to be rebuilt/fortified — symbolic humiliation retained
Prince Karan Singh (Amar Singh's son) attended Mughal court — generational concession strategy
UPSC trap: This treaty is often misread as complete Mewar submission — it preserved key honors that Mewar had fought to retain for 50 years

concepts.name: Architecture of Rajput States: Forts, Palaces, and Distinctive Style
key_dimensions: Amber Fort (Kachwaha) — Sheesh Mahal, blend of Rajput and Mughal architectural elements
Junagarh Fort, Bikaner — no natural elevation, entirely man-made fortification; Karan Mahal inside
Mewar's Udaipur Lake Palace and City Palace — water architecture, Rajput baroque style
UPSC trap: Mehrangarh Fort belongs to Marwar/Jodhpur (Rathores), not Bikaner Rathores — same clan, different forts

concepts.name: Rajput States and the Maratha Expansion (18th Century): Shift in Suzerainty
key_dimensions: Post-Mughal vacuum — Marathas extracted chauth from Rajput states from 1730s onward
Sawai Jai Singh II's failed attempt at Rajput confederation partly aimed at countering both Marathas and Mughals
Rajput states' eventual British subsidiary alliance (early 19th century) as escape from Maratha pressure
UPSC trap: The transition from Mughal to Maratha to British suzerainty over Rajput states is a linear sequence often jumbled in options

concepts.name: Mira Bai: Bhakti Tradition and the Mewar Royal Connection
key_dimensions: Mira Bai — married into Mewar royal family (Rana Sanga's household); devotee of Krishna; conflict with Sisodia orthodoxy
Her compositions (bhajans) in Braj Bhasha — literary and devotional significance
Represents tension between Rajput social norms (honor, kshatriya duties) and Bhakti personal devotion
UPSC trap: Often placed in Gujarat or Rajasthan generically — specifically linked to Mewar Sisodias and later Dwarka tradition

concepts.name: Prithviraj Chahamana (Chauhan) and the Pre-Mughal Rajput State System
key_dimensions: First and Second Battles of Tarain (1191, 1192) — Prithviraj defeated Muhammad of Ghor in First, lost decisively in Second
Why the Second Tarain (1192) is more significant than First Panipat (1526) for Rajput political collapse
Prithviraj Raso (Chand Bardai) as source — bardic tradition, reliability issues, UPSC source-criticism angle
UPSC trap: Prithviraj III (Chahamana) is often confused with the broader Rajput confederacy — he did not represent unified Rajput resistance
